Hybrid attention-SSM architectures — models that interleave Transformer attention layers with state-space model layers (Mamba, S4, etc.) — have become attractive because SSMs offer linear-time sequence processing while attention handles tasks requiring precise token-to-token retrieval. The central question is: when you scale these hybrids (more parameters, longer sequences, larger batch sizes), under what conditions does training become unstable, and why does the instability appear at transitions rather than gradually? The key concepts are the gradient flow mismatch between the two layer types (SSMs use recurrent state updates with learned decay parameters; attention uses softmax normalization), eigenvalue behavior of the SSM's state matrix A as depth increases, and the sensitivity of the gating mechanisms that mediate between the two paradigms. A beginner sees training loss spikes and blames learning rate; an expert worries about the interaction between SSM state initialization and the residual stream statistics, because at scale transitions the residual stream variance can shift enough that the SSM's decay parameters — which were implicitly calibrated to a certain activation scale — enter a regime where gradients through the recurrent path explode or vanish selectively, while the attention layers appear healthy, masking the true source of instability.

In systems like Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023), the state matrix A is parameterized in diagonal form with complex eigenvalues constrained to the unit disk via a softplus reparameterization of the real part — this means individual SSM layers are stable by construction. The problem at depth is compositional: when you stack L SSM layers in a hybrid, the effective state transition across the full residual path is not a single A but an implicit product of L transformations interleaved with nonlinearities and attention outputs, and as L doubles, the spectral radius of this effective composed operator can exit the stable regime even when every individual A is fine. This is qualitatively different from vanilla RNN exploding gradients in two ways: first, vanilla RNN theory (Pascanu et al., 2013) gives you a single recurrent matrix whose eigenvalues you can monitor and clip — the problem is visible in one place; second, in the hybrid case the instability is latent in the interaction between SSM layers and the attention sublayers feeding them, so standard gradient norm monitoring often shows nothing alarming until a spike materializes. Concretely, the attention output at layer k shifts the distribution of inputs to the SSM at layer k+1, effectively perturbing the operating point of that SSM's decay parameters; at scale transitions (say, going from 1.3B to 7B parameters where depth typically increases from ~24 to ~32 layers), this perturbation accumulates multiplicatively across the added layers. What makes it worse is that the imaginary parts of the eigenvalues — controlling oscillation frequency in the SSM's state dynamics — are essentially unregularized, so phase misalignment across stacked layers can produce destructive or resonant interference in the gradient signal that has no analogue in the real-eigenvalue RNN setting.

The dominant practice — Jamba uses 1 attention per 7 SSM layers, Zamba fixes a similar ratio, Samba experiments cluster around 1:4 to 1:6 — is empirically derived and implicitly assumes that the gradient flow balance struck at the ablation scale transfers cleanly to larger models, which it does not. A principled approach would anchor the ratio to the effective gradient path length through the SSM stack between consecutive attention layers: attention acts as a gradient "reset" of sorts because its softmax normalization and value projection re-center the residual stream statistics, so the number of SSM layers between attention layers determines how far the SSM eigenvalue composition problem is allowed to run before it gets interrupted. If you model the per-layer gradient variance contribution of an SSM block as multiplying the residual stream variance by a factor slightly above or below 1 (depending on initialization and current A spectrum), then the tolerable SSM-per-attention count scales roughly logarithmically with depth to keep cumulative variance drift bounded — meaning a ratio that works at 24 layers should compress, not stay fixed, as you go to 32 or 48 layers. What goes wrong when the ratio is held fixed is subtle at first: the model trains without obvious spikes but the SSM layers in the middle of long SSM runs learn progressively shorter effective decay timescales (the A parameters drift toward faster decay) as an implicit self-correction, which means the model is silently sacrificing long-range state retention to stay numerically stable — you see this as degraded performance on long-context tasks rather than as a training crash. The deeper problem is that this drift is irreversible within a training run because the attention layers adapt to the shortened SSM memory horizon, creating a coupled equilibrium that no learning rate schedule or weight decay can undo post-hoc; this is why scale transitions that preserve the ratio tend to produce models that are harder to fine-tune for long-context tasks even when pretraining loss looks acceptable.

The reset function attention provides has two separable components: a statistical reset (re-centering and rescaling the residual stream distribution) and an informational reset (injecting globally-attended context that can correct SSM state drift). GQA and MQA degrade the second component much more than the first — the LayerNorm preceding and following attention handles most of the statistical normalization regardless of head structure, so the distribution re-centering survives the reduction in KV heads largely intact. The informational reset is where GQA's reduced expressivity bites: with full MHA at, say, 32 heads, the attention output is a rank-32 update to the residual stream per token; GQA with 8 KV groups reduces the effective rank of that update, meaning the projection back into the residual stream spans a lower-dimensional subspace and is less able to correct arbitrary SSM state drift directions. Concretely, if the SSM stack has driven the residual stream into an off-manifold region in a subspace that GQA's reduced-rank output doesn't cover, the "reset" is partial — the next SSM layer starts from a partially corrected state, and the composition problem resumes from a worse starting point than it would with full MHA. Empirically this is hard to isolate because GQA is always co-deployed with other efficiency changes, but there's suggestive evidence in the Jamba technical report that attention layer placement sensitivity (which layers can be safely made SSM-only) is higher in models using aggressive KV sharing, consistent with the reset quality degrading. The practical implication is that hybrid models using GQA probably need a lower SSM-to-attention ratio than the equivalent full-MHA model to maintain the same gradient stability margin — a constraint that partially erodes the efficiency gains GQA was supposed to provide, and that nobody currently accounts for explicitly in architecture search.

Adding RMSNorm at the SSM-to-attention boundary does stabilize the residual stream statistics in the short run, but it introduces a specific new failure mode: it breaks the scale signal that the SSM's input-dependent gating (the B and C projection matrices in Mamba's selective scan) relies on to modulate state updates. Those projections are sensitive to input magnitude — they're essentially learning "how much does this token matter for state updates" — and if an interposed RMSNorm collapses magnitude variation before the SSM sees it, the selectivity mechanism degrades toward uniform weighting, which is functionally a regression toward S4-style non-selective dynamics. There's a related problem on the gradient side: RMSNorm's backward pass divides by the forward-pass norm, which can produce very large gradients when the pre-norm activations were small — exactly the regime you're in after a long SSM run that has been quietly compressing activation scale, so the "fix" can induce the gradient spikes it was meant to prevent, just relocated to the normalization layer itself. Empirical evidence for this is indirect but visible in the Mamba-2 design choices (Dao & Gu, 2024): the shift to SSD (structured state-space duality) includes a more careful normalization scheme specifically because naive RMSNorm insertion was observed to hurt selective behavior, and the final architecture uses a grouped normalization that preserves relative scale within feature groups rather than collapsing it globally. The deeper issue is that normalization in SSMs and normalization in Transformers serve different functional roles — in Transformers, LayerNorm is essentially keeping the attention logit scale bounded, while in SSMs normalization touches the recurrent state pathway and must not destroy the dynamic range that selectivity depends on — and hybrid architectures that treat them as interchangeable are conflating two distinct stability requirements that can actively antagonize each other.
